title: Sisaket 3 Days 2 Nights — Khmer Temples, Cliffs & Durian | ThailandAddict
metaDesc: A 3-day, 2-night Sisaket itinerary in Thailand: the Million-Bottle Temple, Sra Kamphaeng Yai Khmer ruins, Pha Mo I Daeng cliff at Kantharalak, and volcanic durian straight from the orchard — with hours, fees and real local eats.
keywords: Sisaket 3 days 2 nights, Sisaket itinerary, Pha Mo I Daeng, Sra Kamphaeng Yai, Sisaket volcanic durian, Million Bottle Temple
h1:
Sisaket in 3 Days, 2 Nights
City, Temples, the Cliff & Durian
intro: Sisaket is the province most people just drive through on the way to Ubon or Surin — even though it has the full set: old Khmer ruins, oddball temples, a border mountain, and volcanic durian grown on genuinely volcanic soil. This 3-day, 2-night plan keeps day one in and around the city, sends you up to Kantharalak on day two for the ruins and the Pha Mo I Daeng cliff, then stops at a durian orchard on the last day before you head home. We've checked opening hours, fees and the latest situation for every stop · Important note: Pha Mo I Daeng and the Khao Phra Wihan park sit right on the Thai–Cambodian border and have been closing on and off because of the border situation, so always check before you set out.

blocks.html: Sisaket town itself is small and walkable, but several of the standout sights are well outside it — especially over in Kantharalak district, which backs onto the Phanom Dong Rak range and the border. It's about 60–65 km from town to Kantharalak, a little over an hour's drive, so we've set day one for the city and the temples close to it, given the whole of day two to Kantharalak, and saved the last day for the durian orchard and souvenirs before the drive home. If you don't have your own car, rent one in town — public transport to the out-of-town sights is thin.

blocks.text: Day 1 — In town, the Million-Bottle Temple, and nearby ruins

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Arrive in Sisaket, see Wat Pa Maha Chedi Kaew, then Sra Kamphaeng Yai

items.activity: Arrive in Sisaket town, check in at your in-town hotel and drop your bags before heading out.
items.note: If you fly into Ubon it's about a 1.5-hour transfer, or take the southern Isan rail line straight to Sisaket station in the middle of town.

items.activity: Drive out to Wat Pa Maha Chedi Kaew (the Million-Bottle Temple) in Khun Han district, where the whole temple is decorated with over a million coloured glass bottles.
items.note: It's about 60 km south of town, free to enter, open daytime daily · the bottles catch the morning sun nicely. If you'd rather not drive far on day one, you can swap this to day two on the way up to Kantharalak.

items.activity: Lunch on punchy Isan food — som tam, grilled chicken, larb — at a place in town or along the way.
items.note: Sisaket takes its Isan food seriously: fermented-fish som tam with real depth, grilled chicken skewers for a few baht each, easy to find all over town.

items.activity: Head to Sra Kamphaeng Yai temple in Uthumphon Phisai district — three sandstone Khmer towers in a row, the oldest and best-preserved ruins in the province.
items.note: About 25–30 km west of town, open 08:00–17:00, entry around 20 THB · the lintels and Khmer carvings are still crisp, best photographed in soft light.

items.activity: Back into town for an evening stroll around the train-station area or the walking street, and dinner in town.
items.note: The evening market and in-town shops have plenty of Isan food — try moo yo, Isan sausage and local sweets.

blocks.title: Day-one tip
blocks.html: Sisaket's sights are fairly spread out — the Million-Bottle Temple is to the south, Sra Kamphaeng Yai to the west. If you'd rather not drive much on day one, do the closer Sra Kamphaeng Yai first and fold the Million-Bottle Temple into day two, since the drive up to Kantharalak passes through the southern zone anyway.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Up to Kantharalak, the ruins and Pha Mo I Daeng

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Ban Prasat ruins – Kantharalak – Pha Mo I Daeng (check the situation first)

items.activity: Leave town early heading south to Kantharalak district, about 60–65 km.
items.note: A little over an hour's drive; the last stretch turns hilly, so fill up the tank before you go — fuel stations get sparse inland.

items.activity: Stop at the Khmer ruins along the way — Ban Prasat or one of the smaller temples on the Kantharalak road — and take in the traces of Khmer civilisation scattered along the border.
items.note: Many of the small ruins are free, unstaffed, and open to wander during the day · good for people who like quiet history with no crowds.

items.activity: Lunch in Kantharalak town — there are several Isan restaurants and noodle shops in the centre.
items.note: Kantharalak is a sizeable district with a decent number of restaurants, cafes and places to stay. If you want to overnight near Pha Mo I Daeng on the second night, staying here is convenient.

items.activity: Go up into Khao Phra Wihan National Park to the Pha Mo I Daeng viewpoint — a tall cliff right on the border, looking out over the Cambodian plain, with ancient bas-relief carvings over 1,500 years old.
items.note: Very important: Pha Mo I Daeng and Khao Phra Wihan park have been closing on and off because of the Thai–Cambodian border situation. Always call the park or check the Khao Phra Wihan National Park page before you set out · if open, entry for Thai visitors is around 20–40 THB.

items.activity: If Pha Mo I Daeng is closed, swap in another spot around Kantharalak — a waterfall, or a durian orchard that's open to visitors — then find a seat for coffee with a mountain view.
items.note: Several durian-orchard cafes around Kantharalak open during durian season, where you can sit and take in the orchard and the Phanom Dong Rak range.

items.activity: Back to Sisaket town, or stay the night in Kantharalak if you'd rather start at the durian orchard the next morning without a long drive.
items.note: If you stay in town it's a little over an hour back · if you stay in Kantharalak you can hit the orchard first thing without the round trip.

blocks.title: Border facts to know before you go
blocks.html: Pha Mo I Daeng and Khao Phra Wihan park genuinely sit right on the Thai–Cambodian border. When tensions rise the park closes the area for safety, and it has stayed shut for months at a time. Don't trust old reviews or pretty photos from past visits — always check the latest announcements from Khao Phra Wihan National Park and the border news first, and have a backup plan in Kantharalak so you're not stuck.

blocks.text: Day 3 — Volcanic durian orchard before heading home

blocks.label: Day 3
blocks.title: Into a Kantharalak volcanic durian orchard, taste it at the source, then buy souvenirs

items.activity: Check out, then head to a volcanic durian orchard around Kantharalak — many open up for in-season tasting and weighing fresh at the orchard.
items.note: Sisaket's volcanic durian season runs roughly late May to August, peaking in June · the well-known orchards are around Trakat sub-district and Ban Sam Ta Rom, with Monthong and other varieties.

items.activity: Taste durian cut fresh off the tree and hear the orchard owner explain why growing on volcanic soil gives drier flesh and a flavour that isn't sharply sweet.
items.note: Retail price at the orchard in season is around 180–250 THB per kilo depending on grade and variety · buying whole is cheaper than pre-packed segments.

items.activity: Settle into an orchard cafe for a light lunch and a rest before the long drive home.
items.note: Some orchards run a cafe and restaurant on site, such as Baan Suan Win Kawa — orchard surroundings with a mountain view, a good stop before you go.

items.activity: Pick up souvenirs — whole durian, rambutan and mangosteen from the orchard, or moo yo and Isan sausage in town.
items.note: If you're carrying durian a long way, ask the orchard to pick a fruit at the right ripeness — tell them the distance and they'll advise which day to eat it.

items.activity: Set off home — via Ubon for a flight, or by train / a long drive back to Bangkok.
items.note: If you're flying back, allow about 1.5 hours to drive to Ubon airport, and always check whether your airline allows durian on board first.

items.name: Baan Suan Win Kawa
items.blurb: A volcanic durian orchard with an on-site cafe in Kantharalak — sit with a coffee over views of the orchard and the range, and in season you can taste durian straight from the tree.

items.name: Suan Thosaphon (Sam Ta Rom)
items.blurb: A volcanic Monthong durian orchard in the Ban Sam Ta Rom area of Trakat sub-district, selling whole fruit and shipping nationwide, with at-orchard prices by grade.

items.name: Suan Mae Si Chan
items.blurb: A Kantharalak volcanic durian orchard selling durian and rambutan in season — contact ahead before visiting.

blocks.text: What to eat in Sisaket — where the locals go

blocks.html: Sisaket is a bold Isan food town — fermented-fish som tam with real depth, smoky grilled chicken, larb and koi, and old-school noodle shops, with plenty to choose from in town. These are the places locals bring up often and that are still open, picked to work as eating pins across the 3-day plan.

items.name: Rom Mai Chai Kha
items.blurb: A relaxed in-town Isan restaurant — crab som tam, larb, grilled fish, free-range chicken tom yam — a full menu the whole family can eat, and a spot locals gather at often.
items.meta: Nong Khrok sub-district, Mueang district · open 08:00–19:00

items.name: Tam Krathoey
items.blurb: A fiery som tam place in town, best known for fermented-fish som tam with real depth, plus yam, curries and fried dishes seasoned hard the way Isan locals like it. One for the spice crowd.

items.name: Pa Somsri Som Tam
items.blurb: An old-school som tam shop across from Sisaket Rajabhat University — big plates, student prices, and a regular haunt for people in the area.

items.name: Tor Tawan
items.blurb: A well-known stewed-pork noodle shop in town — fragrant stewed-spice broth and tender meat, a breakfast or light meal locals are hooked on.

items.name: Grilled chicken & som tam, in-town evening market
items.blurb: Grilled-chicken and som tam stalls in the central evening market — chicken skewers for a few baht each, easy to take back and eat with sticky rice at your hotel, and friendly prices.

items.name: Restaurants in central Kantharalak
items.blurb: On the way up to Pha Mo I Daeng, central Kantharalak has several Isan, noodle and made-to-order spots — a handy lunch pin before heading up the hill.

items.name: Durian-orchard cafes (Win Kawa, etc.)
items.blurb: Cafes set among the volcanic durian orchards around Kantharalak — coffee with orchard and mountain views, and in season you can eat durian fresh on the spot.

items.name: Moo yo & Isan sausage souvenirs
items.blurb: A famous southern-Isan souvenir — dense moo yo and tangy fermented Isan sausage, easy to find in the markets and souvenir shops in town and simple to carry home.

items: Getting around the province — the sights are spread out beyond town, so bring your own car or rent one in town. Sedan rental starts around 800–1,200 THB per day · budget for roughly 150 km of fuel for the round trip up to Kantharalak.

Entry fees — Sra Kamphaeng Yai is about 20 THB, the Million-Bottle Temple and most small ruins are free, and Pha Mo I Daeng / Khao Phra Wihan park is about 20–40 THB when open. The whole trip comes to only a few hundred baht per person.
Volcanic durian — at the orchard in season it's about 180–250 THB per kilo, and buying whole is better value · out of season (September onward) you won't find it fresh anymore.

Where to stay — hotels and guesthouses in Sisaket town start from the low hundreds to the low thousands of baht. Staying in town makes evening food easy, while anyone focused on Pha Mo I Daeng and the durian orchards can stay in Kantharalak on the second night to save driving time.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Sisaket?
faq.a: If you want the town, the Khmer ruins, a trip up to Kantharalak for Pha Mo I Daeng, and a durian-orchard stop, 3 days and 2 nights is about right, because the sights are spread out — town and Kantharalak are about 60 km apart. In a single day you'd only manage the town and the nearby ruins.

faq.q: Is Pha Mo I Daeng open to visitors right now?
faq.a: Pha Mo I Daeng and Khao Phra Wihan National Park sit right on the Thai–Cambodian border, and during periods of tension the park closes the area on and off — it has stayed shut for months at a time. Before you go, always check the latest announcements from Khao Phra Wihan park and the border news, and have a backup plan in Kantharalak ready.

faq.q: When is Sisaket volcanic durian in season?
faq.a: Volcanic durian season runs roughly late May to August, peaking in June, so if you want to taste it at the orchard you need to come in that window. At-orchard prices are around 180–250 THB per kilo depending on grade, and out of season there's no fresh fruit to try.

faq.q: Can you visit Sisaket without your own car?
faq.a: Getting into town is easy by the southern Isan rail line or by flying into Ubon and transferring about 1.5 hours, but for out-of-town sights like Kantharalak and the durian orchards public transport is thin. Renting a car in town or chartering one by the day is far more flexible.

faq.q: Which Khmer ruins in Sisaket are worth seeing?
faq.a: Sra Kamphaeng Yai in Uthumphon Phisai district is the oldest and best-preserved Khmer site in the province, with crisp lintels and carvings. There are also small ruins scattered along the Kantharalak road that are free to enter — good for people who like quiet history.
